text.aria-label: Title text 'Figure 1: At these farms, an XGBoost model given the ENS ensemble mean beats every no-weather baseline to day 5 for solar and to day 7 for wind'
text.tspan: Figure 1: At these farms, an XGBoost model given the ENS ensemble mean
beats every no-weather baseline to day 5 for solar and to day 7 for wind

text.aria-label: Subtitle text 'Every ENS row is an XGBoost model per generator given ENS at that horizon, three ways: the control member; the mean of the 51 members; each member in turn, the 51 forecasts averaged. Each is trained on the input it is scored with. ENS is upsampled to hourly by the combination the rule in Figures 7 and 8 chose: for solar, clear-sky index; for wind, speed from components. No-weather baselines read the telemetry up to 09:00 UTC on the run's own day, when the live service can first read the run, or up to 00 UTC for day 0. Climatology does not depend on the horizon. The two light blue rules are not forecasts: ERA5, and the best past-weather input a live service can read, scored on the same hours. Dot: estimate. Line: 95% interval from resampling whole months and a fitting seed. Capacity is each generator's 99th-percentile output. Six solar farms in Lincolnshire, every daylight hour, April 2024 to September 2026. Three wind farms in Lincolnshire, every hour, August 2024 to September 2026. The intervals are wide mainly because every row's error rises and falls together from month to month; Figures 2, 9, and 10 compare rows on the same months.'
